title: TravelMate
tagline: an interactive travel planning web application

problem.blurb: Use Agile development methodologies to create a travel planning web application in Django.
problem.paragraph: This course focused on teaching Agile software development through collaborative projects. For this project, we were tasked with developing a travel planning application that incorporated external APIs to give users responsive advice based on weather, desired activities, and location. In development, we used the extreme programming (XP) Agile methodology.

overview.summary: Using extreme programming (XP), an Agile software development methodology, my team and I developed a Django web-app for travel planning.
goals: web applications using Agile software methodologies
external APIs to create desired functionalities

background: Agile is a development approach that emphasizes flexibility, collaboration, and customer satisfaction. Several methodologies implement Agile approaches and share a few common values/principles. Agile methodologies are iterative, incremental, and people-centric, creating a more involved relationship with the client and prioritizing strong code outcomes over cost concerns. For this project, we used the extreme programming (XP) methodology, which uses shorter development cycles and minimal documentation.

There are 8 set practices in XP: incremental planning, small releases, simple design, test-first development, refactoring, pair programming, continus integration, and an on-site customer. Adhering to these principles in the short development cycles (in our case, we had 7-day sprints) allowed us to quickly implement features, request feedback, and revise our code accordingly. It is an industry standard methodology for companies like Ford, Chrysler, and IBM.

methods.title: User Stories and Prototyping
methods.summary: Though the class was provided with the same brief concept of the TravelMate app, the specific implementation differed from team to team. We individually developed user stories and low-fidelity prototypes to later present to our teams
methods.description: User stories are a key part of requirements engineering and critical to the incremental plannig practice in extreme programming. Given the one-paragraph concept, I wrote 2 user profiles and 18 user stories describing how those categories of users would interact with the site. These were written in sentence form, first establishing the profile –'As a user'– then describing the feature –'I want to X'– and how the user benefits from the feature –'so that Y'.
media: The paper prototypes helped quickly visualize the implementation of different features and user stories

methods.title: Sprint Planning
methods.summary: We met to assess and consolidate user stories, assign roles, and plan what to accomplish in each sprint. During the project, we performed daily standups of our progress and met weekly with our client/TA to ensure we were satisfying the requested features and our user stories.
methods.description: Having established the user stories and desired end product, we met as a team to assign tasks based on strength, interest, and background. Given my previous experience in web design, my team elected me to oversee the design of the app. However, I also requested some back-end development responsibilities to develop more skills in Django and better translate back-end functionalities to front-end designs.
media: The final project description pulled user stories from our individual proposals

methods.title: Sprint 1
methods.summary: To lay a strong foundation for more complex features, Sprint 1 focused on user stories that connected to multiple features, such as developing the database that would store trip and user data, key features like account registration, and the core travel planning form.
methods.description: For instance, the account registration system (where users can sign up, log in, and reset their account details) was crucial to later user stories like sharing trips between users, saving trips to accounts, and emailing trips externally. We also made sure to implement the trip planning form and fallback pre-determined options to give us adequate time to troubleshoot any issues we had with the SQLite database.
media: Wireframe for Home and Login/SignUp pages

methods.title: Sprint 2
methods.summary: In Sprint 2, we refined the features implemented in Sprint 1, implemented our chosen APIs, refactored for good architecture, and prepared for deployment.
media: The landing page of the finalized site
Trip planning page rendered including API calls

reflection.paragraph: This project introduced me to industry standard approaches to collaborative, user-focused software development by exposing me to Agile methodologies, API integrations, and simulating real-world client feedback. As I continue to develop as a computer scientist, this kind of structured collaboration and public-facing co-creation will help me develop more complex, complete, and coherent creative and academic computing projects.
reflection.futureWork: In the future, I may try other Scrum roles or contribute exclusively to front- or back-end processes, as this project provided foundational knowledge for collaboration industry and academic software engineering contexts.

title: Poetic Alt Text Resource
tagline: A web-based reference on creative and poetic alt text authorship developed for the Fulton County Public Art Futures Lab

problem.blurb: How can we enable artists and curators to write poetic and interpretive alt text for their works?
problem.paragraph: As artistic venues (museums, galleries, etc.) begin to prioritize non-visual accessibility, curators, artists, directors, and docents are seeking resources to better facilitate alt-text/image description authorship in artistic contexts. Though the act of providing alt text is informational, in that it enables Blind/low-vision individuals to equitably experience visual content, there is a level of interpretation, creativity, and subjectivity in the arts that necessitates are more specialized set of guidelines/best practices.

overview.summary: This site was developed as a supplementary resource for the Fulton County Public Art Futures Lab and featured in their celebration of the 36th Anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). It contains written information and interactive practice exercises to empower artists and curators to approach alt text authorship as a creative/poetic/interpretive practice.
goals: existing information about alt text authorship into a single location
considerations of interpretation and creative intent in alt text authorship
with community partners to create public facing living resource(s)

background: Based on initial conversations with the Lab's director about audience and context (artists, curators, and visitors for an in-person event/event series), we decided a digital resource would allow for easy access and dissemination.  Though there are a variety of resources on best practices for alt text in informational and educational contexts, there is little about alt text as a rhetorical and interpretive genre, or as a tool that complements artistic expression.

reflection.paragraph: This was a fascinating application and extension of my previous research and professional experience. With knowledge developed in my accessibility internship and refined in my alt text authorship study, I approached this project with relevant experience and background sources that facilitated strong collaboration with my team, communication with our community partner, and execution of the finished product. Moreover, it was my first opportunity to pursue community-based/public-facing design work and motivated my desire for participatory methods in my work and more accessible means of dissemination.
reflection.futureWork: In the year following this project, I maintained correspondence with the Public Art Futures Lab and consulted on the development of a summer internship protocol to expand the original site's usefulness. Given the time constraints of this project under the course syllabus, there were many unrealized ideas that will significantly improve how this website can be used as an educational community resource. Moreover, this relationship with the Lab was a vital connection in hosting later participatory workshops and design exhibits for other projects.

title: Black Women's Cambridge
tagline: A research-through-design study apply Black feminist geographies to Critical GIS

problem.blurb: How might Black women's geographies disrupt traditional digital GIS practices?
problem.paragraph: Black feminist geographies explain how Black women’s intersectional bodily and emotional experiences of race and gender are expressed in and reinforced by landscapes. They also challenge traditional geographic practices that treat one dominant perspective as an objective truth. Though previous work explores how feminist geographies be used in geographic information systems (GIS) to create more critical, subjective geographic representations, this work often fails to includes Black women's intersectional perspectives.

overview.summary: In this study, I use a research-through-design methodology to locate and visualize Black women’s geographies in ArcGIS, extending previous arguments in feminist GIS to highlight Black feminist geographies. The resulting ArcGIS visualization and design documentation reveals how using ArcGIS with/for Black feminist geographies reveals new critical, qualitative design patterns and possibilities.
goals: Black women's geographies in oral histories
Black women's geographies into critical GIS discourse and research

background: Black women’s sense of place is expressed both under constraints of and in resistance to intersectional oppression, creating an ambiguous, subjective experience of geography  rooted in their embodied and affective relationships with space. “Feminist [and Black] geographers challenge objectivity and mind/body dualisms [of GIS] by recognizing emotion and embodiment as ways of knowing,” emphasizing qualitative data, and rejecting simplification and quantification native to GIS features.  Though work has been done to center both Black and feminist geographic perspectives and approaches to GIS, it is often consolidated under the label of ‘critical GIS’ and continues to neglect intersectionality.

Black women's geographies, McKittrick explains, are entrenched in the poetics of landscape conveyed through creative and expressive acts. Though her book specifically examines plays and novels, I examined oral histories from the Cambridge Public Library archives, locating the geographies expressed by Black women during the interviews and allowing their narratives to guide a counter-mapping of the city of Cambridge and to disrupt the assumptions embedded in ArcGIS and similar software
citations: Demonic Grounds: Black Women and the Cartographies of Struggle

reflection.paragraph: Though I had initial reservations about working in an Urban Studies/Planning lab, this project allowed me to marry my background in archival research with SCL's focus on understanding and visualizing cities through technology. In examining how my current research questions and interests intersect with the built environment, I ultimately devised a project that aligned with my goals and research identity and helped me grow professionally. Though it was fascinating to extend my research and design skill set into a new discipline, I do not see a future for myself in spatial sciences or urban studies. However, the new understanding of Black feminist geographies generated new questions for me about space and place as sites of exploration and investigation in future projects. I also significantly improved my abilities in QDA software, thematic analysis, design documentation, and how to structure a research-through-design project.
reflection.futureWork: This in-depth independent exploration of the field of design, interdisciplinary research, and research-through-design helped me refine my research goals and questions towards speculative design. Though I have enjoyed critiquing and experimenting with the design of existing systems to re-center Black histories, I found myself wondering more during this project what these histories could imply about Black futures. I want to know so much more about what  a future centered on Black experiences, perspectives, and epistemologies looks like. These lessons made me return to GT in Fall 2026 with renewed motivation for my BS/MS application, strong direction for my undergraduate thesis, and a host of new project ideas.

title: 'Uninvited Guests' Remix Ad
tagline: A design fiction advertisement based on a speculative film about assistive technologies, elder care, and autonomy

problem.blurb: What changes when a message changes media?
problem.paragraph: Media does not simply deliver meaning; it shapes meaning. Consider how transforming an existing media artifact into a different medium or format changes its message.

overview.summary: During my Intro to Media Studies course, I was tasked with redesigning an existing media artifact in another medium. I redesigned Uninvited Guests, a speculative film project from the design research firm Superflux, as an editorial advertisement.
goals: an existing artifact in a new medium
the new medium's affordances to convey OR change the original message

background: Uninvited Guests follows Thomas, a 70-year-old widower whose children gifted him smart objects to help him build healthy habits and care for him from a distance. A 'fiercely independent man,' Thomas struggles with the structure the devices impose on his routine and behavior, and we see how he negotiates with the affordances of the technology to maintain his way of life. Fundamentally, the film asks: 'In a world where ’smart objects’ will increasingly be used to provide care at a distance, how will we live with these uninvited guests?'

The film, created in 2015, was intended to elicit reflections and questions about human-technology interaction; how technologies disrupt or enhance existing human behaviors; how they influence and are influenced by human relationships; and, to me, the techno-solutionism of assistive technologies and the importance of co-designing with users to make products that fit more seamlessly into their actual lives, routines, and behaviors.

methods.title: Defining Design Goals and Early Sketches

reflection.paragraph: I chose to reimagine Uninvited Guests as an in-universe print/editorial advertisement for several reasons. Fictional advertisements are frequently used in speculative design to prompt reflection on how we design, produce, market, and consume technology as a commodity. To that end, the medium is well-suited for subliminal/implicit messaging, persuasion, and provocation necessary to present and convince an audience to consider and explore a possible future.
reflection.futureWork: The most difficult part was translating the visual and narrative elements of the film to a single-page advertisement. Primarily, I relied on the more striking visual frames and translated the smartphone overlays to overlapping circles with graphics. I focused on close-up action shots that showed how the technologies would be used, and connected that to the verbiage I used in the advertisements. I decided to illustrate them in Procreate rather than editing in Photoshop because it felt like a more personal approach. In hindsight, Photoshop would have significantly improved the quality of the final advertisement, but this experiment in digital art was better under the time constraints and helped me further challenge myself, which was a significant personal goal for this project. Overall, as an experiment in speculative design and a small-scale project, this piece helped me develop a stronger workflow in digital art and design, consider different media for speculation, and closely examine a work that has fascinated me for a long time.

title: Potluck
tagline: A social media app to foster cultural connection through food for minority college students

problem.blurb: How might we design systems that promote community and connection for marginalized groups?
problem.paragraph: Cultural foods are a critical method of maintaining identity and well-being, but for these students, in unfamiliar cultural environments, they are often unable to cook, share, and consume traditional foods, and to engage in foodways–the cultural behaviors and practices surrounding food. Cultural food insecurity is extremely detrimental to these impacted students, as without the cultural, emotional, and physical connection to their traditional cuisine, they experience feelings of social isolation, anxiety and depression, and severe physical health consequences.

overview.summary: Potluck is a food-focused social media app where users post recipes, finished dishes, and community events to their desired cultural communities.​ It was developed for the Spring 2026 Intro to UI Design course.
goals: an interactive product that improves a population's wellbeing
substantial user research to identify and fill a need

background: This project was intended to address cultural food insecurity among marginalized university students, including ethnic/racial minorities, international students, and first- or second-generation immigrants. Cultural foods are a critical method of maintaining identity and well-being, but for these students, in unfamiliar cultural environments, they are often unable to cook, share, and consume traditional foods and to engage in foodways–the cultural behaviors and practices surrounding food. Cultural food insecurity is extremely detrimental to these impacted students, as without the cultural, emotional, and physical connection to their traditional cuisine, they experience feelings of social isolation, anxiety and depression, and severe physical health consequences. Cultural foods “reinforce a sense of communality” that is vital to the happiness, self-esteem, and social-emotional success of these students at American institutions. Thus, offering these students opportunities to eat foods from their cultures of origin could presumably have positive impacts on their physical and mental health, alleviating reported symptoms and encouraging more nutritional habits.
citations: Eating habits and dietary acculturation effects among international college students in the United States
